lesson.title: Dotted Decimal: Turning 32 Bits Into Something a Human Can Read
lesson.summary: IPv4 address format splits a 32 bit address into four 8 bit octets, each valued 0 to 255, written as dotted decimal notation, a structure that every other IPv4 addressing rule is ultimately built on top of.
lesson.body:
An IPv4 address is, underneath everything, just a single 32 bit binary number, but nobody writes routing tables or configures a router by hand using 32 digit strings of ones and zeros. IPv4 address format is the convention that makes that number usable by people: it splits the 32 bits into four 8 bit groups called octets, converts each octet to its decimal equivalent, and separates the four resulting numbers with periods, a scheme universally known as dotted decimal notation.

Because each octet is exactly 8 bits, it can represent 2 to the 8th power, or 256, distinct values, and since binary counting starts at zero, each octet's valid decimal range runs from 0 to 255, never higher. An address like 192.168.1.1 is really the 32 bit binary string 11000000.10101000.00000001.00000001, grouped into its four octets and converted to decimal for readability; a value like 192.168.1.256 is not a valid IPv4 address at all, because 256 cannot be represented in a single 8 bit octet, it would require a 9th bit.

This four octet structure is not just a notational convenience, it is the foundation that several other IPv4 concepts are built directly on top of. The historical IPv4 address class system looked specifically at the leading bits of the first octet to decide whether an address belonged to class A, B, C, D, or E. The private IPv4 ranges defined in RFC 1918 and the reserved loopback range are both defined as specific values within this same four octet format, for instance the entire 127.0.0.0 through 127.255.255.255 block reserved for loopback traffic. Subnetting, which divides one address block into smaller ones, works by applying a mask across these same 32 bits to separate a network portion from a host portion, and modern classless notation writes that split directly next to the address itself, for example 192.168.1.0/24, where the number after the slash states how many of the leading bits belong to the network.

The four octet boundary also explains a common point of confusion for anyone new to networking: the boundary between octets rarely lines up with the boundary a network actually needs. An organization might need a network sized to exactly 500 hosts, which does not divide evenly along octet lines at all, so subnetting has to operate at the level of individual bits within an octet, not whole octets, to hit that target efficiently.

An IPv4 address can also be written in other bases without changing its meaning at all, since dotted decimal is purely a human readability convention layered on top of the same 32 bit value: the same address can be expressed in full binary as four 8 bit groups, or in hexadecimal, and software frequently converts between these representations internally even though people almost always see the dotted decimal form. What never changes, regardless of how it is displayed, is that an IPv4 address is fundamentally 32 bits of information split into exactly four positions, which is why every rule that governs IPv4 addressing, from address classes to private ranges to subnet masks, is ultimately a rule about how those 32 bits are interpreted.
